answer.rationale: Rollback is off the table: the release carries a non-revertible security patch, so memory_b1's success pattern cannot be applied regardless of how well it worked on day 18. The degradation is explicitly confined to the primary region and is on the write path, which points at regional failover (memory_b2) as the only intervention that addresses the actual locus of the fault. Read-replica routing (memory_b5) relieves read pressure on the primary and would not help a write-path bottleneck; capacity provisioning (memory_b3) worked when pre-provisioned ahead of a known peak, but we are already inside the peak and headroom added now will not land in time; circuit breakers (memory_b4) contained a *dependency* outage by failing fast, which here would shed exactly the settlement writes we are told not to lose. So I verify memory_b2 rather than the alternatives, because it is the single load-bearing record for the action I intend, and its stated conditions differ from today's in the way that matters most: the March degradation says nothing about heavy write volume. A clean traffic shift with error rates recovering in minutes is a much weaker guarantee when writes are at daily peak — in-flight and uncommitted writes are the failure mode the archived summary would not have surfaced. I want the original record to see whether the March event was read-dominant, and whether replication lag or write-drain procedure was measured at all. Because of that gap I scope this as a small guarded shift of write traffic with replication lag and write-acknowledgement monitored before widening, rather than a full cutover on the strength of one consolidated summary. Downstream risk flagged: a failover under peak writes can silently drop customer writes, which is the one outcome the primary objective forbids, and a success here would further entrench 'failover always works' in durable memory even if we got lucky on write drain. If verification shows March was read-heavy or that write-drain was never validated, the correct move is to hold and reassess rather than widen the shift.
